title: DFS in Prague: Can You Reach the Goal Fast?
description: Watch Depth-First Search (DFS) carve a path through a real street-map style graph in Prague’s Žižkov district. The algorithm dives deep along branches first, showing how traversal order changes the route you get.
ig_caption:
🗺️✨ DFS in Prague (Žižkov) — where the next step is chosen by going *deep*, not *short*! 

🧠 What DFS is doing: Depth-First Search explores a graph by taking one branch as far as possible before backtracking. In traversal terms, it’s a classic graph-search method that relies on a “visited” set to prevent cycles and uses a stack/recursion to manage the exploration frontier.

📍 Real street-map vibe: We turn intersections into nodes and streets into edges (a graph), then run DFS to reach a target node. Because DFS prioritizes depth over distance, it may find a valid route quickly—or wander into longer branches—highlighting how traversal order impacts outcomes on real-world networks.

🎬 Your turn: Comment what you think DFS will do next—“go deep first” or “backtrack soon”? Then hit ❤️, share this reel with a fellow coder, and follow for more real-map algorithm visualizations! 🚀

🧭 Depth-First Search (DFS) on a real street-map graph in Prague (Žižkov)! DFS is a graph search technique that goes deep along one path first, then backtracks when it can’t proceed—making its route strongly dependent on neighbor ordering.

📌 This visualization turns intersections into nodes and streets into edges, so you can see how algorithmic exploration works on map-like data. If you learned something new, share this post with a friend who loves coding and comment your favorite part of the traversal!
